theme: Saying what you can (and can't) do — the potential form
intro: Turn any verb into 'can do it' and learn why the object switches from を to が.

grammar.title: The potential form

rules.label: う-verbs (godan)
examples: はなす hanasu → はなせる hanaseru (can speak)
いく iku → いける ikeru (can go)
よむ yomu → よめる yomeru (can read)

rules.label: る-verbs (ichidan)
rules.detail: Drop る and add られる.
examples: たべる taberu → たべられる taberareru (can eat)
みる miru → みられる mirareru (can see/watch)

rules.label: Irregulars
examples: する suru → できる dekiru (can do)
くる kuru → こられる korareru (can come)

grammar.bigPoint: Once a verb is potential, its object usually takes が instead of を: にほんごが はなせます (not を).

examples.jp: にほんごが すこし はなせます。
examples.en: I can speak a little Japanese.

examples.jp: ここで しゃしんが とれますか。
examples.romaji: Koko de shashin ga toremasu ka.

note: Add すこし (a little) or ぜんぜん…ません (not at all): かんじは ぜんぜん よめません = 'I can't read kanji at all.' In casual speech the ら is sometimes dropped (たべれる), but the られる form is the correct, polite standard.

selfCheck.q: How would you say 'I can eat natto (なっとう)'?
selfCheck.a: なっとうが たべられます。 (Nattō ga taberaremasu.) — が because it's the object of a potential verb; たべる → たべられる.
